title: Why Your Brain Aims Attention Before Eyes Move?
description:
Behavioral & Circuit Analysis — Michael Posner (1980): Covert Spatial Attention 'Spotlight' Without Moving Your Eyes, grounded in Michael I. Posner (1980) (Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology). Empirical findings show that in his 1980 Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology classic (7th Bartlett Lecture), Michael Posner asked a deceptively simple question: can you aim your visual attention to the side WITHOUT moving your eyeballs a single millimeter?.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how parietal cortex, thalamus, primary visual cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that participants locked their gaze on a central '+' fixation cross flanked by empty left and right boxes, monitored by electro-oculography (EOG) electrodes beside the eyes so any trial with a real eye movement (>1 degree) was discarded.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Michael I. Posner (1980). Orienting of Attention. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/00335558008248231
- Leah Bakst, Ilona Bloem, Joseph McGuire, Sam Ling (2020). Dynamic spotlight model recovers the position but not the width of covert spatial attention. Journal of Vision. https://doi.org/10.1167/jov.20.11.327
- Amir Raz, Rebecca Oksenhendler (2013). Paying Attention to Michael Posner. PsycCRITIQUES. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0033249

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
